electrodes.name: E6010
electrodes.summary: E6010 is a DC-only cellulosic stick electrode with the deepest penetration of any common rod, used for open-root pipe passes and dirty or rusty steel.
electrodes.meta_description: E6010 runs DCEP only, digs deep, and freezes fast — the standard root-pass rod for pipe. Full specs, amperage by diameter, polarity and storage.

60,000 psi minimum tensile strength of the deposited weld metal
Suitable for all welding positions
High-cellulose sodium coating, DCEP (reverse polarity) only

electrodes.polarity_note: DCEP (electrode positive) only. E6010 will not run on AC or DCEN — the arc stutters and goes out. If you only have an AC buzzbox, use E6011 instead.
electrodes.positions_note: All positions, including vertical-down, which is why pipeline crews use it for stringer beads.

mechanical.impact: 20 ft·lb at -20 °F (27 J at -29 °C)

electrodes.slag: Thin, light, easy to remove
electrodes.arc: Forceful, digging, crisp
applications: Open-root passes on pipe, both shop and field
Pipeline welding with the vertical-down stringer technique
Repair work on rusty, painted, oily or galvanized steel
Tank and pressure vessel root passes
Farm and structural repairs where joint fit-up is poor
characteristics: Deepest penetration of any common mild-steel electrode
Fast-freeze puddle that holds position out of position
Tolerates surface contamination better than low-hydrogen rods
Thin friable slag that mostly peels itself
Noisy, spattery arc compared with E7018

storage.summary: Store at room temperature. Do not bake E6010 — the cellulose coating needs its moisture to work.
details: Keep in the original sealed container at ambient shop temperature.
Coating moisture of roughly 3–7% is by design; that water is the source of the shielding gas.
Baking E6010 in a rod oven drives off the cellulose and ruins the arc characteristics.
If rods have been soaked, discard them — they cannot be reconditioned.

tips: Set the machine 5–10 A higher than you would for E7018 of the same diameter; E6010 likes to be run hot.
Use a tight arc and a whipping motion on the root pass to control the keyhole.
For vertical-down pipe stringers, keep travel speed high enough that the slag never gets ahead of the puddle.
A 1/8 in rod at about 85–95 A is the everyday starting point for open-root work on schedule 40 pipe.

faqs.q: Can E6010 run on AC?
faqs.a: No. E6010 requires DCEP (direct current, electrode positive). The sodium-based cellulosic coating will not sustain an arc on alternating current. E6011 is the AC-capable equivalent.

faqs.q: What is the difference between E6010 and E6011?
faqs.a: They deposit nearly identical weld metal. E6010 uses a sodium coating and runs on DCEP only; E6011 uses a potassium coating and runs on AC or DC. E6010 has a slightly crisper arc and cleaner slag; E6011 is more forgiving on cheap AC machines.

faqs.q: Do you need to bake E6010 rods?
faqs.a: No — never bake them. Unlike low-hydrogen rods such as E7018, E6010 relies on moisture in its cellulose coating to generate shielding gas. Drying them out destroys the arc.

faqs.q: What amperage for 1/8 in E6010?
faqs.a: 70–130 A DCEP, with most root-pass work landing between 80 and 95 A. Go higher for flat fill passes, lower for overhead.

faqs.q: Why is E6010 used for root passes?
faqs.a: Its deep, digging arc reaches through the root opening and fuses the land on both sides, and its fast-freezing puddle stays put in vertical and overhead positions.

electrodes.summary: E6011 is the AC-capable version of E6010 — deep penetration and a fast-freeze puddle that works on small transformer welders and dirty steel.
electrodes.meta_description: E6011 runs on AC or DCEP, digs through rust and paint, and welds all positions. Amperage by diameter, polarity, specs and how it compares to E6010.

characteristics: The default rod for inexpensive AC-only buzzbox welders
Burns through rust, mill scale and paint that would porosity-out a low-hydrogen rod
Fast-freeze puddle for vertical and overhead work
More spatter and a rougher bead face than E6013 or E7018
Deposit is not low-hydrogen, so it is not used on code work requiring low-hydrogen consumables

storage.summary: Room-temperature storage in a dry place. Never bake E6011.
details: Keep sealed until use; a plastic rod tube in a dry shop is sufficient.
The cellulose coating is meant to hold moisture — drying it out kills the shielding action.
Rods with cracked, chipped or swollen coatings should be scrapped.

tips: On a 1/8 in rod, 90–110 A on AC is the everyday starting point for 1/4 in plate.
Whip and pause on vertical-up fillets; drag with a tight arc on flat work.
If the arc sounds like it is popping and hunting, raise the amperage before shortening the arc.
On galvanized steel, weld in ventilated air — zinc fume is a real hazard regardless of the rod.

faqs.q: Is E6011 better than E6010?
faqs.a: Neither is better — they trade places depending on your machine. E6011 runs on AC and DC, which makes it the practical choice on small transformer welders. E6010 runs on DCEP only but gives a slightly crisper arc and cleaner slag, which is why pipeline crews prefer it.

faqs.q: What amperage for 1/8 in E6011?
faqs.a: 75–125 A, with 90–110 A the common working range on 1/4 in mild steel. Drop toward the low end for vertical and overhead passes.

faqs.q: Can E6011 weld through rust and paint?
faqs.a: Yes — that is its main strength. The digging cellulosic arc blows contamination out of the joint. It is still better practice to clean the joint when you can.

faqs.q: Is E6011 low hydrogen?
faqs.a: No. Cellulosic electrodes deposit relatively high diffusible hydrogen by design. For code work on thick or high-strength steel, use a low-hydrogen electrode such as E7018.

faqs.q: What is the tensile strength of E6011?
faqs.a: 60,000 psi minimum tensile strength, with a 48,000 psi minimum yield and 22% minimum elongation in the as-welded condition.

electrodes.name: E6013
electrodes.summary: E6013 is the easy-starting rutile rod for thin steel and light fabrication — soft arc, shallow penetration and the best bead appearance of the 60-series.
electrodes.meta_description: E6013 runs on AC, DCEP or DCEN with a soft arc and shallow penetration — the beginner and sheet-metal rod. Amperage chart, specs and comparisons.

60,000 psi minimum tensile strength
All welding positions
High-titania (rutile) potassium coating, AC, DCEP or DCEN

electrodes.polarity_note: Runs on anything. DCEN gives the shallowest penetration and least burn-through on sheet metal; AC is the most common setting on hobby machines.
electrodes.positions_note: All positions, though it is at its best flat and horizontal.

mechanical.impact: Not required by AWS A5.1 for this classification

electrodes.slag: Heavy, self-lifting, leaves a smooth bead face
electrodes.arc: Soft, quiet, easy to strike and restart
base_metals: Mild steel sheet and light plate
applications: Sheet metal and thin-wall tubing where burn-through is the risk

General light fabrication and shop repairs
Teaching and practice welding — the easiest mild-steel rod to strike
Cosmetic passes where bead appearance matters
characteristics: Very easy arc starting and restarting, even on a cold machine
Shallow penetration — the reason it works on thin material and the reason it is wrong for thick joints
Smooth, finely rippled bead with a flat-to-slightly-convex face
Heavy slag that usually lifts in one piece
Lower elongation requirement than the cellulosic rods, so it is less ductile

storage.summary: Keep dry at room temperature. A sealed container or a warm cabinet is enough — no rod oven required.
details: Rutile coatings absorb moisture slowly and are far less sensitive than low-hydrogen rods.
Damp E6013 causes a hissing arc and worm-track porosity; dry at 250–300 °F (120–150 °C) for an hour if needed.
Store in an unheated shop only if the container is sealed against condensation.

tips: On 16 gauge sheet, a 1/16 in rod at 25–35 A on DCEN keeps you from blowing holes.
Drag the rod with a short arc — E6013 does not need or want whipping.
If the bead is piling up and not wetting the toes, add 10 A rather than slowing down.
Not a substitute for E7018 on structural work; the deposit is not low-hydrogen and the penetration is shallow.

faqs.q: What is E6013 used for?
faqs.a: Thin mild steel and light fabrication — sheet metal, tubing, gates, railings, and general repair. Its soft arc and shallow penetration make it the standard beginner and sheet-metal rod.

faqs.q: What amperage for 1/8 in E6013?
faqs.a: 80–130 A, with 100–115 A typical for 1/8 to 3/16 in plate. On thinner material drop to a 3/32 in rod at 60–80 A.

faqs.q: Is E6013 or E7018 better?
faqs.a: Different jobs. E6013 is easier to run, better on thin material and produces a prettier bead. E7018 is low-hydrogen, stronger, tougher and required on most structural and code work.

faqs.q: Can E6013 weld in all positions?
faqs.a: Yes, the 1 in the classification means all positions. It performs best flat and horizontal; vertical-up work needs the amperage backed off about 10–15%.

faqs.q: Does E6013 need to be kept in a rod oven?
faqs.a: No. Rutile coatings are not low-hydrogen and do not require oven storage. Just keep them dry — a sealed tube in a dry shop is fine.

electrodes.summary: E7014 is an iron-powder rutile rod that runs like E6013 but deposits faster and stronger — a fast-fill, all-position drag rod for production fillets.
electrodes.meta_description: E7014 adds iron powder to a rutile coating for higher deposition at 70 ksi. Runs AC or DC, all positions. Amperage chart, specs and E7018 comparison.

70 ksi deposit instead of the 60 ksi of E6013
Medium penetration — more than E6013, less than E6010
Drag technique: rest the coating on the work and pull
Not a low-hydrogen electrode, so it is not interchangeable with E7018 on code work

storage.summary: Dry room-temperature storage. No oven required, but keep it sealed.
details: Rutile iron-powder coatings tolerate normal shop humidity.
Reconditioning, if needed, is 250–300 °F (120–150 °C) for one hour.
Discard rods whose coating has absorbed enough moisture to flake or swell.

tips: Drag it — a light touch with the coating riding the plate gives the cleanest bead.
For 1/4 in plate fillets, a 1/8 in rod at 130–145 A is a good starting point.
If slag is hard to chip, you are probably running too cold or too slow.
Use E7014 where you would reach for E6013 but need the extra 10 ksi and more fill per rod.

faqs.q: What is the difference between E7014 and E6013?
faqs.a: E7014 has iron powder in the coating, giving a higher deposition rate, medium rather than shallow penetration, and a 70 ksi deposit versus 60 ksi. They run similarly; E7014 simply fills faster and stronger.

faqs.q: Is E7014 low hydrogen?
faqs.a: No. It is a rutile iron-powder electrode. For low-hydrogen requirements use E7018, E7016 or E7028.

faqs.q: What amperage for 1/8 in E7014?
faqs.a: 110–160 A, with 130–145 A typical for 1/4 in plate fillets. Back off 10–15% for vertical and overhead.

faqs.q: Can E7014 be used on structural steel?
faqs.a: It deposits 70 ksi weld metal and is widely used in general fabrication, but most structural codes call for low-hydrogen electrodes on prequalified joints. Check the WPS before substituting it for E7018.

faqs.q: Do you drag or whip E7014?
faqs.a: Drag. The heavy iron-powder coating is designed to be rested against the work and pulled along, which controls arc length automatically.

electrodes.summary: E7018 is the low-hydrogen structural rod — 70 ksi tensile, tough at -20 °F, all positions, and the default electrode on most structural and code work.
electrodes.meta_description: E7018 is the low-hydrogen 70 ksi structural stick electrode. Amperage by diameter, DCEP and AC polarity, rod oven storage rules and full specs.

Smooth, flat-faced beads with good wetting at the toes

storage.summary: Low-hydrogen rods must be kept dry. Hermetically sealed until opened, then held in a rod oven at 250–300 °F (120–150 °C).
details: Store unopened containers at 65 °F (18 °C) or above with relative humidity under 50%.
After opening, hold electrodes in a heated rod oven at 250–300 °F (120–150 °C).
Exposure limits on code work are typically 4 hours for standard E7018 and 9 hours for the H4R moisture-resistant grades — always follow the governing code and the manufacturer's data sheet.
Rods exposed beyond the limit can usually be reconditioned once by baking at 500–800 °F (260–430 °C) for one to two hours.
Never recondition an electrode twice, and never use a rod with a cracked or swollen coating.

tips: Strike ahead of the joint and drag back into the puddle — E7018 tips are prone to sticking on a cold start.
Keep a tight arc, about one electrode diameter, and let the slag trail the puddle.
On 1/4 in plate fillets, a 1/8 in rod at 125–140 A DCEP is the everyday setting.
Vertical-up: reduce amperage 10–15% from flat and use a slight side-to-side motion with a pause at each toe.
If you see wagon-track porosity along the toes, the rod has picked up moisture.

faqs.q: What amperage for 1/8 in E7018?
faqs.a: 110–165 A DCEP. Most shop work on 1/4 in plate runs 125–140 A flat, dropping to about 115–125 A for vertical-up.

faqs.q: Why does E7018 need a rod oven?
faqs.a: Its low-hydrogen coating absorbs moisture from the air. That moisture becomes diffusible hydrogen in the weld, which causes delayed cold cracking in the heat-affected zone. Holding the rods at 250–300 °F keeps the coating dry.

faqs.q: Can E7018 run on AC?
faqs.a: Yes. The 8 in the classification covers AC and DCEP. DCEP gives a more stable arc and easier starts, but E7018 is routinely run on AC transformer machines.

faqs.q: Can you weld vertical-down with E7018?
faqs.a: Not on code work. The heavy slag runs ahead of the puddle going downhill and causes slag inclusions and lack of fusion. E7018 is run vertical-up.

faqs.q: How long can E7018 stay out of the oven?
faqs.a: Typically 4 hours for standard E7018 and up to 9 hours for H4R moisture-resistant grades, but the governing code and the manufacturer's data sheet set the actual limit.

faqs.q: What is the difference between E7018 and E7018-1?
faqs.a: E7018-1 meets a lower-temperature impact requirement, 20 ft·lb at -50 °F instead of -20 °F, and has a slightly higher minimum elongation. Chemistry and handling are otherwise the same.

electrodes.summary: E7024 is a heavy iron-powder drag rod for flat and horizontal fillets only — the fastest-depositing common stick electrode, sometimes called a jet rod.

Not low-hydrogen

Reconditioning is 250–300 °F (120–150 °C) for one hour if the rods get damp.

faqs.q: Why is E7024 sometimes called a jet rod?
faqs.a: It is a trade nickname for the heavy iron-powder drag electrodes. The thick coating forms a deep crucible at the tip, so the rod can be dragged at high speed with a very smooth arc.

faqs.q: Can you weld vertical with E7024?
faqs.a: No. The 2 in the classification limits it to the flat position and horizontal fillets. The large fluid puddle will sag out of position.

faqs.q: What amperage for 1/8 in E7024?
faqs.a: 140–190 A, with roughly 160–175 A typical on 3/8 in plate fillets.

faqs.q: Is E7024 stronger than E7018?
faqs.a: Both are 70 ksi minimum tensile. E7018 is tougher and low-hydrogen; E7024 deposits faster but has shallow penetration, lower ductility and no low-temperature impact requirement.

faqs.q: What is E7024 used for?
faqs.a: Long flat and horizontal fillet welds on heavy plate where deposition rate is the priority — shipbuilding, structural shops and beam fabrication.

electrodes.summary: E308L is the standard stick electrode for welding 304 and 304L stainless, with a low 0.04% maximum carbon that protects against intergranular corrosion.
electrodes.meta_description: E308L-16 welds 304 and 304L stainless steel. Low carbon prevents carbide precipitation. Amperage by diameter, polarity, ferrite and storage specs.

Deposit retains a small amount of delta ferrite, typically FN 4–10, which resists hot cracking
Slower-freezing puddle than carbon steel electrodes
Roughly half the thermal conductivity and 50% more thermal expansion than carbon steel, so distortion control matters
Higher electrical resistance means the rod heats up along its length — run it cooler and shorter

storage.summary: Keep dry. Stainless coatings pick up moisture and cause porosity and worm tracks.
details: Store unopened in a dry area; after opening, hold at 250–300 °F (120–150 °C) in a rod oven.
Redry damp electrodes at 500–600 °F (260–315 °C) for one hour — check the manufacturer's data sheet, as stainless redry temperatures are lower than carbon steel low-hydrogen rods.
Never store stainless rods loose in a toolbox with carbon steel rods; iron contamination causes rust spotting on the finished weld.

tips: Run 10–15% lower amperage than you would use on carbon steel of the same thickness.
Keep interpass temperature below about 350 °F (175 °C) to limit sensitization and distortion.
Use stainless-only brushes and grinding media; carbon steel contamination will rust and initiate pitting.
Chip all slag completely — stainless slag left between passes is a classic source of inclusions.
For 304 to carbon steel joints, use E309L instead; E308L will dilute to a crack-sensitive composition.

faqs.q: What is E308L used for?
faqs.a: Welding Type 304 and 304L austenitic stainless steel — food and dairy equipment, chemical piping, tanks and architectural work.

faqs.q: What does the L in E308L mean?
faqs.a: Low carbon, 0.04% maximum. Less carbon means less chromium carbide forms at the grain boundaries when the weld is held in the 800–1500 °F range, which preserves corrosion resistance.

faqs.q: Can E308L weld 316 stainless?
faqs.a: It will make a sound weld mechanically, but it has no molybdenum, so the joint loses the pitting and chloride resistance that 316 is chosen for. Use E316L on 316 base metal.

faqs.q: What amperage for 1/8 in E308L?
faqs.a: 65–110 A DCEP, typically around 80–95 A. That is noticeably lower than a 1/8 in carbon steel rod because stainless conducts heat poorly and the electrode overheats.

faqs.q: Can you weld stainless to carbon steel with E308L?
faqs.a: No — use E309L. Dilution from the carbon steel side drops the alloy content of an E308L deposit into a martensitic, crack-sensitive range.

electrodes.summary: E309L is the dissimilar-metal electrode — its extra chromium and nickel survive dilution when joining stainless to carbon steel or laying a stainless overlay.

faqs.q: What is E309L used for?
faqs.a: Welding stainless steel to carbon steel, laying the first buffer layer of a stainless overlay, welding 309 base metal, and repairing unknown or hard-to-weld steels.

faqs.q: Why use E309L instead of E308L for dissimilar joints?
faqs.a: Melting carbon steel into the puddle dilutes the alloy content. E309L starts with about 23% chromium and 12% nickel, so after dilution it still contains enough ferrite to resist hot cracking. An E308L deposit diluted the same way turns martensitic and cracks.

faqs.q: What amperage for 1/8 in E309L?
faqs.a: 65–110 A DCEP, commonly 80–95 A. Use the low end and stringer beads to keep dilution down.

faqs.q: Can E309L weld 304 to 304?
faqs.a: Yes, it will make a sound and corrosion-resistant weld, but it costs more than E308L and offers no advantage on a matching joint.

faqs.q: Is E309L magnetic?
faqs.a: Slightly. The deposit contains delta ferrite, which is ferromagnetic, so a magnet will show weak attraction. That is expected and is what keeps the weld from hot cracking.

faqs.q: What is the difference between E316L and E308L?
faqs.a: E316L contains 2–3% molybdenum, which greatly improves resistance to pitting and crevice corrosion in chloride environments. E308L has none. Use E316L on 316/316L base metal and in marine or chemical service; use E308L on 304/304L.

faqs.q: What amperage for 1/8 in E316L?
faqs.a: 65–110 A DCEP, typically 80–95 A. Stainless rods run cooler than carbon steel because of their low thermal conductivity and high electrical resistance.

faqs.q: Can E316L weld 304 stainless?
faqs.a: Yes. It is over-alloyed for 304 and will make a sound, corrosion-resistant weld — it just costs more than E308L with no benefit unless chlorides are present.

faqs.q: Why does 316L stainless need a back purge?
faqs.a: Without an inert purge on the back side of a root pass, the hot chromium-rich surface oxidizes into a rough gray scale called sugaring, which destroys corrosion resistance and cannot be fixed by brushing.

faqs.q: Is E316L food grade?
faqs.a: 316L weld metal is widely used in food, dairy and pharmaceutical equipment. Suitability for a specific installation depends on the finish, cleaning and the governing sanitary standard, not on the filler alone.

faqs.q: What is the difference between E347 and E308L?
faqs.a: E347 is stabilized with niobium, which locks up carbon permanently. E308L simply keeps carbon low. For long service in the 800–1500 °F sensitization range, stabilization holds up better; for ordinary ambient-temperature corrosion service, E308L is adequate and cheaper.

faqs.q: Why is 321 stainless welded with 347 filler?
faqs.a: Type 321 is stabilized with titanium, but titanium oxidizes and does not survive transfer across the welding arc. Niobium does, so 347 filler delivers the same stabilizing effect in the weld metal.

faqs.q: What amperage for 1/8 in E347?
faqs.a: 65–110 A DCEP, typically around 80–95 A.

faqs.q: Is E347 more crack sensitive?
faqs.a: Slightly. Stabilized chemistries are a little more prone to hot cracking than plain 308. Keep heat input modest, use stringer beads, and do not let interpass temperature climb.

faqs.q: Can E347 be used on 304 stainless?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is a good choice when 304 will see extended elevated-temperature service. For ordinary room-temperature corrosion resistance, E308L is the standard filler.

faqs.q: Does E410 require preheat?
faqs.a: Yes. Preheat of 350–450 °F (175–230 °C) is required and must be maintained as interpass temperature. The deposit air-hardens to martensite and will crack without it.

faqs.q: Does E410 need post-weld heat treatment?
faqs.a: For almost all structural and pressure applications, yes — typically tempering at 1200–1400 °F (650–760 °C) followed by controlled cooling. Hardfacing overlays are sometimes left as-welded where the hardness is the point.

faqs.q: Is E410 magnetic?
faqs.a: Yes. Martensitic stainless is strongly magnetic, unlike the austenitic 300-series deposits from E308L, E309L or E316L.

faqs.q: What amperage for 1/8 in E410?
faqs.a: 70–110 A, typically around 90 A. Keep heat input controlled and maintain the preheat temperature throughout.

faqs.q: Can E410 be used without heat treatment?
faqs.a: Only for hardfacing overlays on thin sections where hardness is wanted and the joint is not load-bearing in tension. On any structural joint, skipping PWHT leaves brittle, crack-prone weld metal.

faqs.q: Can you stick weld aluminum?
faqs.a: Yes, with covered aluminum electrodes such as E4043 under AWS A5.3, but the results are markedly worse than TIG or MIG. The process is limited to flat position, the flux is corrosive, and porosity is common. It is a field-repair method, not a production one.

faqs.q: What is the difference between E4043 and ER4043?
faqs.a: E4043 is a flux-covered stick electrode for SMAW; ER4043 is bare wire or rod for MIG and TIG. Both deposit the same 5% silicon aluminum chemistry, but ER4043 gives cleaner, stronger, more controllable welds.

faqs.q: Why does aluminum stick welding need preheat?
faqs.a: Aluminum conducts heat roughly four times faster than steel, so heat runs out of the joint before fusion is established. Preheat of 300–400 °F on thick sections keeps enough heat in the weld zone.

faqs.q: Does the flux need to be removed after welding?
faqs.a: Yes, completely. The salt-based flux residue is corrosive and will attack the aluminum. Wash with hot water and scrub with a dedicated stainless brush.

faqs.q: What is the tensile strength of E4043 weld metal?
faqs.a: AWS A5.3 sets a minimum of 14,000 psi as-welded for E4043 covered electrodes. Bare ER4043 filler deposited by TIG or MIG typically reaches a higher value under cleaner conditions.

faqs.q: What is the difference between ER70S-6 and ER70S-3?
faqs.a: ER70S-6 has more silicon and manganese, so it tolerates mill scale, rust and surface oxides better and wets out flatter. ER70S-3 is fine on clean steel and costs slightly less. Most shops stock only ER70S-6.

faqs.q: Can ER70S-6 be used as a TIG rod?
faqs.a: Yes. The ER prefix means it qualifies as both a continuously fed electrode and a hand-fed rod, and it is commonly sold in 36 in TIG lengths.

faqs.q: What settings for 0.035 in ER70S-6 on 1/8 in steel?
faqs.a: Roughly 19–20 V with 250–280 ipm wire feed in short-circuit transfer on C25 gas, which works out near 140–160 A. Fine-tune by sound and bead profile.

faqs.q: Can you weld rusty metal with ER70S-6?
faqs.a: Light mill scale and surface rust, yes — that is what the extra silicon and manganese are for. Heavy rust, paint or oil will still cause porosity; grind the joint clean when you can.

faqs.q: What is the difference between ER308L and E308L?

faqs.q: Do you need to back purge when welding 304 with ER308L?

faqs.q: What amperage for 1/16 in ER308L TIG rod?

faqs.q: Can ER308L weld 316 stainless?

faqs.a: Roughly 70–130 A DCEN, with about 70–90 A on 1/8 in material and up toward 130 A on 1/4 in.

faqs.q: Does ER316L need to be back purged?
faqs.a: On pipe and tube roots, yes. Oxidation on the unshielded side forms sugaring, a rough gray scale that cannot be repaired without cutting the joint out.

faqs.q: Is ER316L suitable for saltwater?
faqs.a: It resists chlorides far better than 304-grade fillers, which is why it is standard for marine work, but it is not immune. For severe seawater service, specifiers move to duplex, super-austenitic or nickel alloys.

electrodes.name: ER4043
electrodes.summary: ER4043 is the 5% silicon aluminum filler — fluid, crack-resistant and the default choice for welding 6061 and aluminum castings.
electrodes.meta_description: ER4043 is 5% silicon aluminum TIG rod and MIG wire for 6061 and castings. Crack resistant, AC TIG settings, amperage chart and ER5356 comparison.

classification_breakdown.meaning: Electrode or rod — usable for MIG or TIG
Aluminum Association alloy 4043, nominally 5% silicon, balance aluminum

electrodes.polarity_note: TIG on aluminum uses AC so the reverse half-cycle strips the oxide layer. MIG uses DCEP, usually through a spool gun or push-pull torch because the soft wire birdnests in a standard liner.
electrodes.positions_note: All positions with TIG or pulsed MIG. Aluminum's fluid puddle makes out-of-position work demanding; pulsed transfer helps considerably.

mechanical.impact: Not applicable

electrodes.deposition: High on MIG, moderate on TIG
electrodes.slag: None; remove the oxide layer mechanically before welding
electrodes.arc: Fluid and fast, with a narrow window between cold and burn-through

options.note: Standard for both TIG and MIG on aluminum up to about 1/2 in.
Adds heat for thicker sections and improves wetting.
Heavy plate and castings where penetration is the limit.

shielding_gas.flow: 20–30 CFH (9–14 L/min); aluminum needs more coverage than steel

applications: Welding and repairing 6061 structures, frames and extrusions
Casting repair on engine blocks, housings and manifolds
General aluminum fabrication where strength is not the limiting factor
Heat exchangers and tubing in 3003
Anywhere crack sensitivity outweighs the need for joint strength
characteristics: 5% silicon lowers the melting point and widens the freezing range, which is what makes it crack resistant
More fluid than ER5356 — easier to run, wets out flatter
Finishes dull gray and turns dark if the part is anodized, so it is the wrong choice for cosmetic anodized work
Lower shear and tensile strength than ER5356
Not recommended for 5xxx base metals containing more than about 3% magnesium, where Mg-Si compounds embrittle the weld

storage.summary: Keep sealed and dry. Aluminum filler grows an oxide layer and picks up moisture that turns into weld porosity.
details: Store TIG rod in a sealed tube; keep MIG spools bagged with desiccant when out of the machine.
Handle with clean gloves — hydrogen from skin oils and moisture is the main cause of aluminum weld porosity.
Wipe rods with acetone and use a dedicated stainless brush on the joint immediately before welding.
Do not use filler that has developed a visible white oxide bloom.

tips: On AC TIG, set balance around 65–70% electrode negative for good penetration with enough cleaning action.
Preheat sections over 1/4 in to 250–300 °F (120–150 °C), but never exceed 400 °F on heat-treatable alloys.
Clean with a stainless brush dedicated to aluminum immediately before welding — the oxide reforms in minutes.
For MIG, use a spool gun or push-pull torch with a nylon or graphite liner; a steel liner shaves the soft wire.
Choose ER4043 when the part might crack and ER5356 when the joint needs strength or will be anodized.

faqs.q: What is the difference between ER4043 and ER5356?
faqs.a: ER4043 is 5% silicon: more fluid, more crack resistant, easier to weld, but weaker and it anodizes dark gray. ER5356 is 5% magnesium: stronger, better color match when anodized, stiffer to feed, and more sensitive to cracking on some base metals.

faqs.q: Can ER4043 weld 6061?
faqs.a: Yes — it is the standard filler for 6061. The silicon suppresses the hot cracking that a matching 6061 filler would suffer from.

faqs.q: What gas do you use with ER4043?
faqs.a: 100% argon for both TIG and MIG on material up to about 1/2 in. Argon-helium mixes add heat for thicker sections and castings.

faqs.q: Why does aluminum TIG use AC?
faqs.a: Aluminum carries a tough oxide skin that melts far hotter than the metal beneath it. The electrode-positive half of the AC cycle blasts that oxide off, while the electrode-negative half puts heat into the joint.

faqs.q: Will ER4043 match the color after anodizing?
faqs.a: No. A 4043 weld anodizes dark gray to black against the base metal. For cosmetic anodized work, ER5356 gives a much closer match.

electrodes.name: ER5356
electrodes.summary: ER5356 is the 5% magnesium aluminum filler — stronger than ER4043, stiffer to feed, and the choice when the joint must carry load or be anodized.
electrodes.meta_description: ER5356 is 5% magnesium aluminum wire and TIG rod: higher strength than 4043 and a color match when anodized. Amperage, gas and service temperature limits.

classification_breakdown.meaning: Electrode or rod — usable for MIG or TIG
Aluminum Association alloy 5356, nominally 5% magnesium with small chromium and manganese additions

electrodes.polarity_note: AC for TIG to provide oxide cleaning; DCEP for MIG. ER5356 is stiffer than ER4043 and feeds noticeably better through a long gun.
electrodes.positions_note: All positions. The slightly less fluid puddle makes out-of-position work easier than with ER4043.

mechanical.impact: Not applicable

electrodes.deposition: High on MIG, moderate on TIG
electrodes.slag: None; mechanical oxide removal required before welding
electrodes.arc: Slightly stiffer and less fluid than ER4043

options.note: Standard for TIG and MIG up to about 1/2 in.
Extra heat for thick plate and better wetting.
Heavy sections where argon alone runs out of penetration.

applications: Boat hulls, marine structures and 5083/5086 plate
Structural aluminum joints where shear strength governs the design
Trailers, truck bodies and tanks
Parts that will be anodized and need a color match
Aluminum bicycle and motorcycle frames
characteristics: Roughly 40% higher tensile strength than ER4043 and much better shear strength in fillet welds
Anodizes to a near match with common base alloys, where 4043 goes dark gray
Stiffer wire feeds better through long MIG guns and push-pull systems
More sensitive to hot cracking on high-silicon base metals and castings than ER4043
Not recommended for sustained service above about 150 °F (65 °C), where magnesium above 3% can sensitize and lead to stress corrosion cracking

storage.summary: Sealed and dry. Magnesium-bearing aluminum oxidizes readily and moisture becomes weld porosity.
details: TIG rod in a sealed tube, MIG spools bagged with desiccant.
Handle with clean gloves — skin oils are a hydrogen source.
Wipe with acetone before welding and brush the joint with a dedicated stainless brush.
Discard filler showing a white powdery oxide bloom.

tips: Use it on 5xxx base metals and wherever a fillet weld's shear strength governs the design.
For anodized work, ER5356 is the only sensible choice of these two fillers.
Preheat over 1/4 in to 250–300 °F (120–150 °C); avoid prolonged heat on 5083/5086 in marine service.
Avoid it on high-silicon castings such as 356 — magnesium plus silicon in those proportions cracks; use ER4043 there.
Feed problems usually mean liner and drive-roll setup, not the wire: use U-groove rolls and a nylon or graphite liner.

faqs.q: Is ER5356 stronger than ER4043?
faqs.a: Yes. ER5356 runs about 38 ksi tensile against roughly 27 ksi for ER4043, and its shear strength in fillet welds is substantially higher. That is why structural and marine work specifies 5356.

faqs.q: Which filler anodizes better, 4043 or 5356?
faqs.a: ER5356. A 4043 weld anodizes dark gray to black and stands out sharply; 5356 comes much closer to the base metal color.

faqs.q: Can ER5356 weld 6061?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is preferred when the joint's strength governs. ER4043 is the more crack-tolerant choice on restrained 6061 joints and castings, so the selection depends on whether strength or crack resistance matters more.

faqs.q: Why is ER5356 not used above 150 F?
faqs.a: Aluminum alloys with more than about 3% magnesium can sensitize during long exposure to elevated temperature, precipitating a magnesium phase at grain boundaries that makes the metal vulnerable to stress corrosion cracking.

faqs.q: Why does ER5356 feed better than ER4043?
faqs.a: It is a harder, stiffer alloy. Soft 4043 wire buckles and birdnests in the drive rolls on a long gun, while 5356 pushes through more reliably.

electrodes.name: E71T-1
electrodes.summary: E71T-1 is gas-shielded flux-cored wire — the high-deposition, all-position production workhorse for structural steel, combining FCAW speed with a smooth spray-like arc.
electrodes.meta_description: E71T-1 gas-shielded flux-cored wire: all-position 70 ksi deposits with high deposition rates. Gas, amperage by diameter, CTWD and AWS A5.20 specs.

classification_breakdown.meaning: Electrode
70,000 psi minimum tensile strength
All welding positions
Tubular (flux-cored) wire
Rutile slag system, gas shielded, DCEP, with 20 ft·lb impact toughness at 0 °F

electrodes.polarity_note: DCEP. This is the opposite of self-shielded T-11 wire, which runs DCEN — getting the polarity backwards is the most common setup mistake when switching between the two.
electrodes.positions_note: All positions. Vertical-up is standard on structural work; some manufacturers qualify vertical-down procedures for specific wires.

mechanical.impact: 20 ft·lb at 0 °F (27 J at -18 °C); -1J and -1M grades extend this to -20 °F

electrodes.coating: Rutile flux core inside a mild steel sheath
electrodes.deposition: Very high — roughly twice the rate of a comparable stick electrode
electrodes.slag: Fast-freezing rutile slag that supports the puddle out of position and peels readily
electrodes.arc: Smooth, spray-like, with a fine droplet transfer

options.note: Deeper penetration, lower gas cost, more spatter. The classic choice for structural work.
Smoother arc, less spatter, slightly higher deposition efficiency and better out-of-position control. Higher tensile than the same wire on CO2.

shielding_gas.flow: 35–45 CFH (16–21 L/min). FCAW-G needs more flow than solid-wire MIG, and it cannot be used outdoors without a windscreen.

applications: Structural steel fabrication and erection
Shipbuilding and barge construction
Heavy equipment and earthmoving machinery
Pressure vessel fill and cap passes
Any indoor production joint where deposition rate drives cost
characteristics: Deposition rates far above stick and above solid MIG wire at equal amperage
The slag system holds the puddle for genuine all-position welding at high current
Requires external shielding gas — wind over about 5 mph will cause porosity
Higher fume generation than solid wire; good local exhaust matters
Slag must be removed completely between passes or inclusions result

storage.summary: Keep dry. The flux core absorbs moisture through the seam of the wire, and damp wire means porosity and hydrogen cracking.
details: Store unopened spools in a dry area at normal shop temperature.
Once a spool is opened, either use it or return it to a sealed bag with desiccant, or hold it in a heated cabinet at 250–300 °F (120–150 °C).
A spool left on the machine over a humid weekend will often show porosity in the first several feet — run it off before starting critical work.
Surface rust on the sheath means the spool should be discarded.

tips: Use a contact-tip-to-work distance around 3/4 to 1 in — considerably longer than solid-wire MIG.
Drag the gun with a 5–15 degree drag angle so the slag trails the puddle.
For 0.045 in wire on plate, about 26–28 V and 300–350 ipm is a solid starting point on CO2.
Knurled drive rolls with light tension — a tubular wire crushes if you clamp it like solid wire.
Do not use FCAW-G outdoors without a windscreen; if you need wind tolerance, switch to a self-shielded wire such as E71T-11 or E71T-8.

faqs.q: What gas do you use with E71T-1?
faqs.a: 100% CO2 or 75% argon / 25% CO2. CO2 penetrates deeper and costs less; the argon mix gives a smoother arc, less spatter and better out-of-position control.

faqs.q: Is E71T-1 DCEP or DCEN?
faqs.a: DCEP, electrode positive. Self-shielded wires such as E71T-11 run DCEN, so the polarity must be changed when switching between the two types.

faqs.q: What is the difference between E71T-1 and E71T-11?
faqs.a: E71T-1 is gas shielded, runs DCEP, and produces tougher, higher-quality welds suitable for code work. E71T-11 is self-shielded, runs DCEN, needs no gas bottle, and tolerates wind — but has lower toughness and is usually thickness limited.

faqs.q: What settings for 0.045 in E71T-1?
faqs.a: Roughly 26–28 V with 300–350 ipm wire feed on CO2, which works out around 250–300 A. Use about 3/4 in contact tip to work distance.

faqs.q: Can E71T-1 be used outdoors?
faqs.a: Not without shelter. It depends on external shielding gas, and wind above about 5 mph blows the gas away and causes porosity. Use a self-shielded flux-cored wire outdoors.

electrodes.name: E71T-11
electrodes.summary: E71T-11 is self-shielded flux-cored wire — no gas bottle, runs DCEN, and works in wind, which makes it the standard gasless wire for small machines and outdoor repair.
electrodes.meta_description: E71T-11 self-shielded flux-cored wire needs no shielding gas and runs DCEN. Settings by diameter, thickness limits, and how it compares to E71T-1.

classification_breakdown.meaning: Electrode

electrodes.positions_note: All positions, and unusually it is often run vertical-down on thin material, which is where many hobby users work.

mechanical.impact: Not required by AWS A5.20 for the -11 classification

electrodes.coating: Self-shielding flux core inside a mild steel sheath
electrodes.slag: Heavy and fast-freezing; peels off but leaves more to clean than gas-shielded wire
electrodes.arc: Somewhat harsh with visible spatter, especially at low settings

options.note: The flux core generates its own shielding gas and slag. Adding gas is unnecessary and will not improve the weld.

shielding_gas.flow: Not applicable. Remove or bypass the gas solenoid connection when converting a MIG machine to gasless operation.

applications: Outdoor and windy-site repair welding
Farm, ranch and trailer repair
Hobby and home-shop welding on small 120 V machines
Field maintenance where carrying a gas bottle is impractical
Welding on rusty, painted or galvanized steel
characteristics: No shielding gas required — the main reason it is chosen
Wind tolerant, unlike solid MIG wire or gas-shielded flux core
More spatter and smoke than any gas-shielded process
No impact toughness requirement, and most manufacturers limit it to single or limited multi-pass work on material under about 1/2 in
Runs DCEN, which is the reverse of both solid MIG wire and E71T-1

storage.summary: Keep dry and sealed. Self-shielded flux core is hygroscopic and damp wire is the usual cause of porosity on gasless machines.
details: Bag opened spools with desiccant, or store them in a heated cabinet.
A spool left exposed in a humid garage will produce porosity within weeks.
Run several feet off before starting real work on a spool that has been sitting.
Discard wire with visible rust on the sheath.

tips: Check the polarity first — more gasless welding problems trace to DCEP than to anything else.
Use a longer stickout than solid wire, roughly 1/2 to 3/4 in.
Drag the gun, never push — pushing rolls the slag ahead of the puddle and traps it.
Expect to chip slag; the appearance will never match gas-shielded MIG, and that is normal.
For thicker plate or any code work, move to E71T-1 with gas or to a low-hydrogen stick electrode.

faqs.q: Does E71T-11 need shielding gas?
faqs.a: No. The flux inside the tubular wire generates its own shielding gas and slag cover, which is what makes it usable outdoors and on machines with no gas bottle.

faqs.q: Is E71T-11 DCEN or DCEP?
faqs.a: DCEN, electrode negative. Most small MIG machines ship set up for DCEP solid wire, so the gun and work leads must be swapped. Wrong polarity gives an erratic, spattery arc.

faqs.q: How thick can you weld with E71T-11?
faqs.a: Manufacturers commonly limit it to material under about 1/2 in, and many restrict it to single-pass or limited multi-pass welds. Check the specific product data sheet — the limits vary by brand and are a real restriction, not a suggestion.

faqs.q: Why does my gasless flux core weld look so bad?
faqs.a: Usually one of four things: reversed polarity, too short a stickout, pushing instead of dragging the gun, or damp wire. Self-shielded wire also produces more spatter than gas-shielded processes even when everything is right.

faqs.q: Can E71T-11 be used on structural steel?
faqs.a: It has no impact toughness requirement and is usually thickness limited, so it is generally not used for structural code work. E71T-1 with gas, or E7018, is the appropriate choice there.
